source_text: Frivolam sane expositionem in hoc loco tuam optimo iure despicerem et irrepercussam praeterirem, quasi nimis humo cohaerentem, nisi vererer, ne pellaciae magis quam constantiae crederetur. Loqueris ergo hoc modo: Quid est: " Multo magis abundavit " [n134] , nisi quia omnes, qui per Christum liberantur, temporaliter propter Adam moriuntur, propter ipsum autem Christum sine fine victuri sunt? [n135] Quo sermone si, quid consequenter diceretur, attenderes, omnem arcem tuam id est traducem cecidisse faterere; dicis enim ideo multo magis abundasse Christi gratiam, quia per eam vita conferatur aeterna, cum per Adae peccatum subeunda sit corruptio temporalis. Si ergo nihil aliud intulit Adam praeter corporis mortem, contra quem Christus copiosiore beneficio vitam contulit sine fine durantem, apparet non peccatum Adae ad posteros transisse, sed mortem.
pass_a_gloss: I would with best right despise your frivolous exposition in this place and pass it by unanswered, as clinging too much to the ground, unless I feared that it would be credited to evasion rather than to constancy. You speak therefore in this way: What is: 'It abounded much more,' except because all who are freed through Christ die temporally on account of Adam, but on account of Christ himself they are about to live without end? By which speech if you attended to what would be said consequently, you would confess that your whole citadel, that is the tradux, had fallen; for you say that for this reason the grace of Christ abounded much more, because through it eternal life is conferred, when through Adam's sin a temporal corruption must be undergone. If therefore Adam brought in nothing else besides the death of the body, against whom Christ conferred by a more copious benefit a life lasting without end, it appears that not Adam's sin passed to posterity, but death.

lemmas.lexica: LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'
LS mors; Blaise temporal vs eternal death in Rom 5

pass_b_english: I could very properly despise your trifling explanation of this passage and pass it over unanswered, as lying too low on the ground, if I did not fear that this might be credited to evasion rather than confidence. You speak as follows: ‘What does “abound much more” mean (Romans 5:15), except that everyone freed through Christ dies a temporal death on account of Adam, but will live without end on account of Christ himself?’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.46). If you considered what follows consistently from this statement, you would confess that your entire fortress—that is, inherited transmission—had fallen. For you say Christ’s grace abounded much more because through it eternal life is conferred, whereas through Adam’s sin temporal decay must be undergone. If, then, Adam brought nothing but bodily death, in contrast with which Christ conferred the more generous benefit of life without end, it appears that what passed to descendants was not Adam’s sin but death.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied.
